subject: Svenska 2
title: Rhetorical analysis
sourceSummary: Analysing real speeches using rhetorical concepts — modes of appeal, figures of speech and the six parts of classical disposition — as well as the difference between giving a speech and analysing one.

questions.prompt: Which part of the classical speech disposition has the task of addressing and dismissing counterarguments?
questions.explanation: Confutatio (also called refutatio) is the part of the speech where the speaker addresses and refutes the opponent's arguments. Propositio presents the speaker's main thesis, and peroratio is the conclusion.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between narratio and argumentatio in the classical disposition?
questions.opener: One part narrates what happened, another part persuades.
choices: They are synonymous terms for the introduction of the speech
Narratio recounts the background and the facts of the matter, argumentatio presents evidence for the speaker's thesis
Narratio is the conclusion, argumentatio is the introduction
questions.explanation: Narratio provides background information and recounts the state of affairs, while argumentatio is the part in which the speaker presents their arguments and evidence for their position.

questions.prompt: "We came, we saw, we conquered." Which figure of speech is this phrasing built on?
questions.opener: Count the parts — how many are there, and what happens to the rhythm?
questions.explanation: A tricolon is a list of three parts that creates rhythm and emphasis — a classic example is Caesar's "veni, vidi, vici". Metonymy, by contrast, involves replacing a word with a closely related concept.

questions.prompt: "That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind." The sentence is built on which figure of speech by setting "small" against "giant" and "a man" against "mankind"?
questions.opener: Two opposites are set against each other for effect.
questions.explanation: Antithesis involves setting opposites against each other to create contrast and emphasis. The phrasing is built precisely on the contrast between the small and the great.

questions.prompt: What is the most important difference between giving a speech and analysing a speech?
questions.opener: One role persuades, the other examines.
choices: Analysis is only about summarising the content of the speech
Giving a speech is about persuading an audience, analysing a speech is about examining HOW the speaker tries to persuade
Giving a speech requires no rhetorical concepts, but analysis does
questions.explanation: When giving a speech, one uses rhetorical means to persuade an audience. When analysing a speech, one instead steps back and examines which means (modes of appeal, figures of speech, disposition) the speaker uses and why they work — or do not work.

questions.prompt: A speaker chooses to give a speech about equality on International Women's Day. Which rhetorical concept describes the importance of choosing the right occasion for a speech?
questions.explanation: Kairos is about choosing the most fitting moment or context for a message — speaking about equality precisely on Women's Day strengthens the speech's impact.

questions.prompt: Greta Thunberg's speech at the UN Climate Action Summit in 2019 had a huge impact even though the speaker was young and previously unknown to most listeners. Analyse which rhetorical means nonetheless give the speech strong impact.
questions.opener: Consider what can compensate for a lack of formal authority.
questions.answer: The speech gains power through an unusual combination of strong pathos (an angry, emotionally charged tone), repetitions that build up an escalating crescendo, and an ethos built up through the speaker's personal credibility as a representative of an entire generation rather than through formal expertise.
steps: The speaker's ethos is not built on traditional authority (age, title or expert knowledge), but on moral credibility as a representative of young people affected by climate change.
Pathos is prominent through the angry, emotionally charged tone that conveys seriousness and urgency to the listeners.
Repeated, accusatory phrasings gradually build up the intensity towards the end of the speech, which is an example of anaphora.
The combination of personal pathos and a clearly structured escalation makes the speech memorable despite the absence of traditional formal authority.

questions.prompt: Summarise the six parts of the classical speech disposition.
questions.opener: From greeting to closing appeal — six steps.
questions.answer: Exordium: the introduction that captures attention and builds goodwill · Narratio: background and an account of the state of affairs · Propositio: the speaker's thesis or main message · Argumentatio: arguments and evidence for the thesis · Confutatio (refutatio): addressing counterarguments · Peroratio: a summarising and emotionally charged conclusion meant to stay with the audience.

questions.prompt: Which mode of appeal is built on logic, facts and rational arguments?
questions.opener: The name of this mode of appeal is the root of the English word "logic".
questions.explanation: Logos is built on logic, facts, statistics and rational reasoning to persuade. Ethos instead concerns the speaker's credibility, and pathos concerns stirring the audience's emotions.

questions.prompt: Which mode of appeal concerns the speaker's credibility and character?
questions.opener: The word is also the root of the English word "ethics".
questions.explanation: Ethos concerns the speaker's credibility, character and authority — why the audience should trust this particular speaker. Logos is instead built on facts and logic, and pathos on emotions.

questions.prompt: "Time heals all wounds" is an example of which figure of speech, where an abstract concept is given a human ability?
questions.opener: Time itself cannot literally "heal" anything — a human action is attributed to the concept.
questions.explanation: Personification means something non-human, here the abstract concept of time, is given a human characteristic or ability, such as being able to heal. Anaphora instead concerns repetition at the start of sentences.

questions.prompt: Which figure of speech involves repeating the same word or phrase at the beginning of several consecutive sentences or clauses?
questions.opener: The repetition builds a rising rhythm through the speech.
questions.explanation: Anaphora is the repetition of the same word or phrase at the beginning of several consecutive sentences or clauses, which creates rhythm and emphasis. A tricolon is instead specifically a list of three parts.

questions.prompt: Which part of the classical disposition is the very first part of the speech, meant to capture the audience's attention and build goodwill?
questions.opener: The word means roughly "that which leads out" or "introduction" in Latin.
questions.explanation: Exordium is the introduction of the speech, whose purpose is to capture the audience's attention and build goodwill towards the speaker before the rest of the speech continues. Peroratio is instead the conclusion of the speech.

questions.prompt: When analysing a speech's ethos, what exactly are you examining?
questions.opener: The focus is on the speaker as a person, not the logic of the arguments or the audience's emotional state.
choices: How the speaker builds up their credibility, for example through experience, expertise or moral character
Only which figures of speech the speaker uses
Only how long the speech is
Only which day the speech was given
questions.explanation: An analysis of a speech's ethos examines how the speaker builds up their credibility, for example by demonstrating experience, expertise, moral character or personal integrity. Figures of speech, the length of the speech, and which day it was given are other kinds of analytical questions.

questions.prompt: "He's not exactly the fastest" when you actually mean he is very slow. Which figure of speech is this an example of?
questions.opener: You say less than you mean, often with an ironic undertone.
questions.explanation: Litotes is an understatement, often with an ironic effect, where you say less than you actually mean — here it's implied that the person is very slow by saying they're "not exactly" fast.
